subject.title: To Quilca, a Country House not in Good Repair
subject.author: Jonathan Swift
subject.text:
Let me thy Properties explain,
A rotten Cabin, dropping Rain;
Chimnies with Scorn rejecting Smoak;
Stools, Tables, Chairs, and Bed-steds broke:
Here Elements have lost their Vses,
Air ripens not, nor Earth produces:
In vain we make poor Sheelah toil,
Fire will not roast, nor Water boil.
Thro' all the Vallies, Hills, and Plains,
The Goddess Want in Triumph reigns;
And her chief Officers of State,
Sloth , Dirt , and Theft around her wait.

title: The Insult License That Ran Out
standfirst: Swift's twelve lines about a collapsing Irish farmhouse were the gentlest kind of mockery he wrote about its owner. A promise the two men made years earlier — to always report each other's failings honestly — is what eventually ended the friendship.

sections.heading: A Cat Stood Trial for the Missing Bacon
sections.body:
Before Jonathan Swift compressed his complaints about Quilca into twelve lines, he had already spent a whole essay on the subject. *The Blunders, Deficiencies, Distresses, and Misfortunes of Quilca*, begun on 20 April 1724, is a mock-scholarly inventory of everything wrong with Thomas Sheridan's farmhouse in County Cavan, proposed, as a joke about how much material there was, as the first of a projected [twenty-one quarto volumes](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Works_of_the_Rev._Jonathan_Swift/Volume_8/Blunders,_Deficiencies,_Distresses,_and_Misfortunes_of_Quilca). It records "but one lock and a half in the whole house," a lost garden-door key, and Swift's own greatcoat pressed into service stopping a window that would not shut. It also records a cat, caught raiding the cellar, "tried, condemned, and executed by the sword" — full mock-legal procedure for a household too broke to simply shoo it away.

A year later Swift wrote the poem the reader has just read, and it turns out to be the same complaint run through a wringer until only the bones were left: a roof that drops rain, chimneys that reject smoke, and poor Sheelah the servant unable to get fire to roast anything or water to boil. Twelve lines instead of a mock-multivolume essay, but built from the same house, the same running joke, and the same specific target — a friend, not a stranger, being needled in public.

sections.heading: A School on Capel Street, an Estate by Marriage
sections.body:
The friend was Thomas Sheridan, a Trinity College Dublin graduate who ran one of Dublin's better-regarded schools, on Capel Street, teaching the children of prominent families through the 1720s. Quilca was not his by birth; it came to him through his father-in-law, a small property near Mullagh in County Cavan that he treated, by every account, as somewhere between a retreat and a burden. Swift and Sheridan had by then settled into the kind of friendship that ran on hospitality in both directions: Sheridan a regular guest at the Deanery in Dublin, Swift a [repeat visitor to Quilca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sheridan_%28divine%29) between 1722 and 1725, long enough to know exactly which locks didn't work.

That two-way traffic matters, because it is what makes the poem's mockery affectionate rather than cruel. Swift was not reviewing somebody else's failing investment from a safe distance; he was describing a house he kept choosing to stay in, about a man whose company he kept choosing to seek out, in a form built to be read aloud back to its target and laughed at together.

sections.heading: Two Opposite Verdicts, Filed Under One Year
sections.body:
Swift did not even commit to a single opinion of Quilca. The manuscript that carries this poem also carries two companion pieces, both dated [1725](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Works_of_the_Rev._Jonathan_Swift/Volume_7/To_Quilca): "The Blessings of a Country Life" and "The Plagues of a Country Life." The Blessings side praises exactly the isolation the main poem complains about — "Far from our debtors; no Dublin letters; / Nor seen by our betters" — while the Plagues side lists a different, more specific set of grievances: gossiping company, missing shoes, thin food, empty pews, servants who simply leave. Read together, the three poems don't build toward a verdict on Quilca. They run the same joke from both directions at once and let the contradiction stand.

The main poem's own form does something similar in miniature. Each rhymed couplet runs long enough to make a proper complaint, then a short one-word or one-image line lands after it like a shrug — "In his own ground," "In winter fire" — a stanza shape built to undercut its own seriousness before it can accumulate into a real grievance. It is a poem engineered not to be taken entirely at its word, which turns out to be exactly the kind of poem Swift and Sheridan's friendship ran on.

sections.heading: The Milky Battle, Fought for Stella's Health
sections.body:
Quilca's disrepair was not only a joke for Swift. He brought Esther Johnson — Stella, his closest companion — and her chaperone Mrs Dingley on his visits there, and the same *Blunders* essay records a genuine domestic crisis over her: a "milky battle" between the household's servants, who refused to milk the cows before eleven in the morning, and the requirements of [Mrs Johnson's health](https://www.libraryireland.com/biography/ThomasSheridanDD.php), which needed the milk earlier. It is one of the essay's funniest lines and one of its least jokey facts at the same time.

The house left other, gentler marks. A century and more later, local memory in Mullagh still pointed to a stand of hawthorns as ["Stella's Bower,"](https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/5070796/5064633/5096120) and to a beech-lined walk — the "Dark Walk" — as ground Swift had personally supervised the planting of. And it was at this same leaking, understaffed, badly-locked farmhouse, in this same year, that Swift finished *Gulliver's Travels*. Whatever else was wrong with Quilca, it was where one of the most completely realised satires in English got its final work done, milky battles and all.

sections.heading: One Bible Verse, Two Different Occasions
sections.body:
Sheridan's own career took the kind of hit Swift only ever inflicted on him in verse. He had been made a royal chaplain, a real step toward preferment, and lost it over a single sermon. The accounts of exactly when and why do not fully agree. One biographical dictionary states plainly that [he preached at Cork on the King's birthday](https://www.libraryireland.com/biography/ThomasSheridanDD.php); the *Dictionary of National Biography* instead dates it to a Sunday that fell on [1 August](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Sheridan,_Thomas_%281687-1738%29_%28DNB00%29) — the anniversary of Queen Anne's death and, not incidentally, of George I's accession. Both agree on the text he chose: "Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Preached on a day the court was marking as a cause for celebration, that verse reads less like piety than commentary, and a Whig courtier named Richard Tighe made sure it was heard that way, reporting it as confirmation "that the preacher was a Jacobite."

Whichever occasion it actually was, the effect is not in dispute: Sheridan was struck from the chaplains' list and barred from court, and Swift's own attempt to intercede on his behalf failed. A man who spent his spare time trading mock complaints about a leaking roof had just watched his real career collapse over one honest, badly timed sentence.

sections.heading: The Promise Nobody Was Meant to Keep
sections.body:
Years into the friendship, Sheridan made Swift a private promise: he would always tell him honestly when he saw signs of avarice creeping into his character. It is exactly the kind of arrangement two men who traded rhymed insults about each other's houses might make, half in earnest, over a slow evening at Quilca. Sheridan, unlike most people who make such promises, appears to have actually kept notes. Eventually he handed Swift a written record of everything he had observed, in his own hand, rather than just mentioning it in passing.

Swift's recorded reply was a question: had Sheridan [never read *Gil Blas*](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Sheridan,_Thomas_%281687-1738%29_%28DNB00%29)? The reference is exact and unflattering to Swift himself. In Lesage's novel, the Archbishop of Granada extracts precisely this promise from his secretary — "as soon as you shall be of opinion that my head is not so clear as usual, give me warning of it instantly" — and when Gil Blas eventually, honestly, tells him a recent sermon fell short "of the overpowering eloquence and conclusive argument of your former ones," the Archbishop erupts — "I have been finely taken in by your outside shew of cleverness, without any solid foundation of sober judgment!" — and dismisses him with a purse of money and an icy blessing: "God speed you, good Master Gil Blas! I heartily pray that you may do well in the world!" Swift knew the book well enough to reach for it instantly. That he reached for it to describe his own reaction, rather than to catch himself before having one, is the whole story in a single allusion.

sections.heading: The Coat Stayed in the Window; the Friendship Didn't
sections.body:
The break, when it came, arrived through a visit rather than a single confrontation. In 1738 Sheridan had given up his school and gone to stay at the Deanery; he fell seriously ill there, and once he had recovered, Swift told him he was [no longer welcome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Sheridan_%28divine%29). The exact trigger is disputed, but the avarice ledger sits near the center of most accounts of it, and the two things Swift is recorded objecting to about Sheridan in his final years — an overlong stay, and an unwanted honesty about his character — are not obviously separable. Sheridan died a few months later, on 10 October 1738, at dinner in a house in Rathfarnham, without the two men having properly reconciled.

The house at Quilca is where their friendship's actual rule got written, even if nobody wrote it down as such: mockery, freely traded, aimed at a leaking roof or a blunted spit or a servant's failed milking schedule, was not just tolerated between them but practically the currency of their affection. A greatcoat stuffed in a window, a cat court-martialled for stolen bacon, a poem that undercuts its own complaints with a shrugging short line — all of it said, in effect, that nothing said in that register could really wound. The promise to report each other's real faults, honestly and in writing, was the one clause outside that register. It is the one that ended things.
